topic: France grew from Roman Gaul and the Frankish kingdom of Clovis and Charlemagne into a kingdom built up piece by piece by the Capetian kings around Paris.
From Louis XIV it was Europe's most powerful state and the centre of its culture; the Revolution of 1789 overthrew the monarchy and spread the ideas of citizenship and nationhood.
Between 1789 and 1958 France tried monarchies, empires and five republics, and fought three wars with Germany (1870, 1914, 1939).
Since 1945 it has lost its colonial empire, become a founding member of the European Union and a nuclear power, under the Fifth Republic founded by de Gaulle.

Prehistory: Humans have lived in France for hundreds of thousands of years; its caves (Lascaux, Chauvet) hold some of the oldest art in the world.
Farming spread from about 6000 BC; the Bronze Age brought the Bell Beaker culture and metalworking.
Celtic Hallstatt and then La Tène cultures dominated by the Iron Age: the peoples the Romans called Gauls.
Ancient history: Greek traders founded Massalia (Marseille) around 600 BC.
Rome took southern Gaul in the 120s BC, and Julius Caesar conquered the rest in the Gallic Wars (58–50 BC), defeating Vercingetorix at Alesia in 52 BC.
Gaul became thoroughly Roman, with Latin, cities and roads; from the 400s Germanic peoples (Visigoths, Burgundians, Franks) crossed the Rhine and carved it up.
Frankish kingdoms (486–987): Clovis I united the Franks, defeated the last Roman ruler Syagrius (486) and the Visigoths (507), and converted to Catholic Christianity.
Charles Martel stopped an Umayyad army near Tours (732); his son Pepin the Short became king, founding the Carolingian dynasty.
Charlemagne built an empire across western Europe and was crowned emperor in Rome by Pope Leo III in 800.
The Treaty of Verdun (843) split the empire among his grandsons; West Francia, under Charles the Bald, became France.
State building into the Kingdom of Franc: Hugh Capet founded the Capetian dynasty in 987, ruling little more than the land around Paris.
Kings slowly gained ground: Philip II Augustus took Normandy from King John and won at Bouvines (1214); Philip IV clashed with the pope and moved the papacy to Avignon.
The Hundred Years' War (1337–1453) with the English kings, who claimed the French throne, brought defeats at Crécy, Poitiers and Agincourt.
Joan of Arc relieved Orléans in 1429 and had Charles VII crowned; by 1453 the English held only Calais.
Early Modern France (1453–1789): Francis I fought the Habsburgs in the Italian Wars and patronised the Renaissance; the Wars of Religion (1562–98) ended with Henry IV's Edict of Nantes.
Richelieu and Mazarin built royal power and won the Thirty Years' War against the Habsburgs.
Louis XIV (1643–1715) ruled as an absolute monarch from Versailles, and France became Europe's dominant power and cultural model.
18th-century wars cost France most of its first colonial empire and its finances, while Enlightenment writers questioned the old order.
Revolutionary France (1789–1799): Bankruptcy forced Louis XVI to call the Estates-General in 1789; the Third Estate declared itself the National Assembly and Paris stormed the Bastille.
The Declaration of the Rights of Man abolished feudal privilege; the monarchy fell in 1792 and Louis XVI was executed in 1793.
War with Europe and internal revolt brought the Terror (1793–94) under Robespierre, then the Directory.
General Napoleon Bonaparte seized power in the coup of 18 Brumaire (1799).
Napoleonic France (1799–1815): Napoleon ruled as First Consul and then Emperor from 1804; the Napoleonic Code and centralised administration outlasted him.
His armies dominated continental Europe until the invasion of Russia in 1812 failed.
Defeated at Leipzig (1813), he abdicated; he returned for the Hundred Days in 1815, lost at Waterloo, and the Bourbons under Louis XVIII were restored.
1815–1914: Revolutions in 1830 and 1848 overthrew two monarchies; the Second Republic elected Louis-Napoleon, who made himself Napoleon III (Second Empire, 1852–70).
Defeat by Prussia in 1870–71 lost Alsace-Lorraine and ended the Empire; the Third Republic followed after the Paris Commune was crushed.
The Republic built secular schools, separated church and state (1905), expanded the empire and allied with Russia and Britain (the Triple Entente).
Colonial empire: France's second colonial empire grew from Algeria (1830) to most of West and North Africa, Indochina and Madagascar.
It was the second largest empire in the world, justified by a 'civilising mission'.
After 1945 it came apart through the First Indochina War (lost at Dien Bien Phu, 1954), the Algerian War (to 1962) and African independence around 1960.
1914–1945: France bore much of the Western Front in the First World War and lost about 1.4 million soldiers; it won back Alsace-Lorraine in 1918.
In 1940 Germany defeated France in six weeks; the north was occupied and Marshal Pétain's Vichy regime collaborated.
Charles de Gaulle led the Free French from London; France was liberated in 1944.
Since 1945: The Fourth Republic rebuilt the economy (the 'Trente Glorieuses') but fell over the Algerian War in 1958.
De Gaulle founded the Fifth Republic with a strong presidency, ended the Algerian War in 1962 and gave France its own nuclear force.
The protests of May 1968 shook the regime; since then presidents from Giscard to Mitterrand, Chirac and their successors have led France deeper into European integration.
